definition: The equation that CPU execution time equals instruction count × cycles per instruction × clock period. It shows that clock speed alone does not predict performance: all three terms matter.
example: 2 × 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.5 on a 3 GHz clock take exactly 1 second.

definition: The number of instructions a program actually executes in a run (the dynamic count), not the number of lines or instructions in its code. A loop of 3 instructions run a million times counts 3 million.
example: Halving IC at the same CPI and clock halves the run time.

definition: Cycles per instruction: total clock cycles divided by instructions completed over a run. An average, not the latency of any one instruction; below 1 on cores that finish several instructions per cycle.
example: 3 × 10⁹ cycles for 2 × 10⁹ instructions is a CPI of 1.5.

definition: Instructions per cycle: instructions completed divided by clock cycles, the reciprocal of CPI. Often quoted for modern cores because they can complete more than one instruction per cycle.
example: perf stat showing 6 billion instructions in 3 billion cycles reports 2.00 IPC (CPI 0.5).

definition: The duration of one clock cycle, the reciprocal of the clock frequency. In a pipeline it must fit the slowest stage plus pipeline-register overhead.
example: A 3 GHz clock has a period of about 0.333 ns; a 200 ps period is a 5 GHz clock.

definition: How many clock cycles a processor runs per second, measured in hertz. Higher is not automatically faster, because cycles per instruction and instruction count also matter.
example: A 3 GHz core ticks 3 × 10⁹ times per second.

definition: One tick of the processor clock: the basic unit of time in which pipeline stages do their work and pipeline registers latch new values.
example: In the five-stage pipeline each instruction spends one clock cycle in each stage.

definition: The time a processor spends executing a particular program or thread, as distinct from wall-clock time, which also includes waiting for I/O and other programs.
example: A program can take 4 s of CPU time but 10 s of wall-clock time if it waits on the disk.

definition: Real elapsed time from start to finish, as a clock on the wall would measure it, including any time spent waiting rather than computing.
How many times faster one version is than another: the old (or other) run time divided by the new one. 1.5 means "50% faster", not "50% less time".
example: 0.667 s versus 0.6 s is a speedup of about 1.11.

definition: The proportions of different instruction classes (ALU operations, loads, stores, branches) that a program executes. In a simple model, CPI is the mix-weighted average of each class's cycle cost.
example: A mix of 50% ALU at 1 cycle, 20% loads at 5, 10% stores at 3 and 20% branches at 2 gives CPI 2.2.

definition: MIPS as a performance metric: instructions executed per second, in millions. Misleading across compilers or ISAs, because it ignores how many instructions the task needs.
example: 1.2 × 10⁹ instructions in 1.2 s is 1,000 MIPS.

definition: Floating-point operations per second, a measure of numerical throughput. Vendors usually quote the peak, which real code rarely sustains.
The mistaken belief that a higher clock frequency alone means a faster processor, ignoring cycles per instruction and instruction count.
The counting mode of perf, the Linux performance-analysis tool: `perf stat` runs a program and reports hardware counters such as cycles, instructions, IPC, branches and branch misses.
example: perf stat -e branches,branch-misses ./prog counts branch mispredictions.

definition: Special registers in a CPU that count hardware events such as cycles, instructions retired, cache misses and branch mispredictions, read by tools like perf.
How a particular processor implements an instruction set: its pipeline, caches, predictors and execution units. Two chips with the same ISA can have very different microarchitectures and CPI.
The manufacturing technology used to make a chip, especially the size of its transistors. Each new generation typically makes transistors smaller, denser and faster.
Complex instruction set computer: an ISA style with many complex, variable-length instructions, some of which access memory or do several steps at once. x86 is the main example.
example: x86 rep movsb copies a whole block of memory with one instruction.

definition: Reduced instruction set computer: an ISA style with simple, regular, usually fixed-length instructions in which only loads and stores touch memory. This regularity makes pipelining easier.
example: RISC-V, MIPS and ARM are RISC instruction sets.

definition: The CISC instruction set family used by most Intel and AMD PC and server processors. Instructions are 1 to 15 bytes long, so modern implementations translate them into micro-operations before pipelining them.
An open, royalty-free RISC instruction set, widely used in teaching and increasingly in real chips. Its base instructions are 32 bits long, and register x0 always reads as zero.
example: lw x1, 8(x2) loads the word at address x2 + 8 into x1.

definition: A RISC instruction set from the 1980s whose classic five-stage pipeline is the standard teaching model in the Patterson and Hennessy textbooks. Its register 0 is hard-wired to zero and classic versions have a branch delay slot.
The 64-bit Arm instruction set (AArch64), a RISC ISA used in most phones and many laptops and servers. It has no branch delay slots and offers csel for conditional selection.
Arithmetic logic unit: the circuit that performs integer arithmetic and logic operations such as add, subtract, AND and compare. In the five-stage pipeline it works in the EX stage.
A hardware block that carries out one kind of operation, such as an integer ALU, a multiplier, a floating-point adder or a load-store unit. Wide cores have several of each.
The functional unit that executes loads and stores: it computes addresses and accesses the data cache.
Program counter: the register holding the address of the instruction being fetched. Branch predictors are indexed by bits of the PC.
example: In RISC-V, IF computes PC + 4 as the next sequential address.

definition: The small, fast array of a processor's registers, with ports for reading operands and writing results. Wide cores need many ports, which makes it large and power-hungry.
The part of a machine instruction that says which operation to perform, such as add or load.
Widening a signed binary number by copying its sign bit into the new high bits, so its value is unchanged. ID sign-extends an instruction's immediate value before EX uses it.
example: The 12-bit value 0xFFF sign-extends to the 32-bit value −1.

definition: A small, fast cache holding recently used instructions, read by the fetch stage. Bigger code, for example from loop unrolling, can cause more instruction-cache misses.
A small, fast cache holding recently used data, read and written by loads and stores in the MEM stage.
An access to data or instructions that are not in the cache, so they must come from a slower level. A miss that has to go all the way to main memory can cost hundreds of clock cycles on a fast core.
example: An 80 ns miss at 4 GHz costs 320 cycles.

definition: A design with one main memory but separate instruction and data caches, so instruction fetch and data access can happen in the same cycle. It removes the classic memory structural hazard.
A circuit that selects one of several inputs to pass to its output, according to a control signal. Forwarding uses multiplexers in front of the ALU inputs.
Logic whose output depends only on its current inputs, with no memory. Its delay sets how long a pipeline stage must be.
The difference in arrival time of the same clock edge at different parts of a chip. It must be budgeted in the clock period.
How long a register's input must be stable before the clock edge for the value to be captured reliably. It adds to the overhead of every pipeline register.
The instant the clock signal switches (usually from low to high), when registers capture their inputs.
Overlapping the execution of several instructions by splitting each into stages, so a new instruction can start every cycle. It raises throughput, not the speed of a single instruction.
example: A five-stage pipeline has up to five instructions in flight at once.

definition: One step of a pipeline, taking one clock cycle. The classic RISC pipeline has five: IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB.

Instruction fetch: reading the next instruction from memory (normally through the instruction cache) at the address in the PC. In the five-stage pipeline it is the first stage, which also computes the next sequential PC.
Instruction decode, the second pipeline stage: work out what the instruction is, read its source registers and sign-extend any immediate value.
Execute, the third pipeline stage: the ALU performs the operation or computes a load/store address.
Memory access, the fourth pipeline stage: loads read and stores write the data cache.
Write back, the fifth pipeline stage: the result is written into the destination register.

A register between two pipeline stages that captures, at each clock edge, everything the instruction needs next: operand values, destination register and control signals. Named after the stages it separates.
example: The ID/EX register holds the operands that EX will use next cycle.

definition: A processor that executes each instruction completely in one long clock cycle, which must fit the slowest instruction. Simple, but most of the hardware sits idle.
The start and end of a run, when some stages are empty because the pipeline is still filling with instructions or emptying. A k-stage pipeline needs k − 1 extra cycles for this.
Stages that take equal time. Because the clock must fit the slowest stage, unbalanced stages waste time in the faster ones and limit speedup.
A pipeline that starts at most one instruction per cycle, so its CPI can never fall below 1.
Instructions that all have the same size (32 bits in base RISC-V), so fetch always knows where the next one starts. x86 instead has variable-length instructions of 1 to 15 bytes.
An ISA in which only load and store instructions access memory; arithmetic works only on registers. It keeps memory access in one pipeline stage.
Placing a value at an address that is a multiple of its size, such as a 4-byte word at an address divisible by 4. Aligned accesses never straddle two cache lines.
A simple, RISC-like internal operation that a processor decodes complex instructions into. x86 cores pipeline and schedule µops rather than raw x86 instructions.
A situation that stops the next instruction starting in its pipeline slot. The three kinds are structural, data and control hazards.
A hazard where two instructions need the same piece of hardware, such as a single memory port, in the same cycle.
A hazard where an instruction needs a result an earlier instruction has not produced yet (or the order of register reads and writes could go wrong).
A hazard caused by branches: the processor does not yet know which instruction to fetch next until the branch is resolved.
Holding an instruction in place for one or more cycles until it can proceed safely; each stall cycle inserts a bubble and adds to CPI.
example: Without forwarding, an add followed by a dependent sub needs two stall cycles.

definition: An empty, do-nothing slot moving through the pipeline, inserted by the hardware during a stall or left behind when an instruction is flushed. It behaves like a NOP instruction, but no instruction was fetched for it.
Read after write: a later instruction reads a register an earlier one writes, so data really flows between them. It cannot be renamed away, only waited for or forwarded.
example: add x1, x2, x3 then sub x4, x1, x5 is a RAW dependence on x1.

definition: Write after read: a later instruction overwrites a register an earlier one still needs to read. A name dependence, removed by register renaming.
Write after write: two instructions write the same register and the final value must be the later one's. A name dependence, removed by register renaming.
An ordering constraint (WAR or WAW) that exists only because two instructions reuse a register name, not because data flows between them.

Also called forwarding or bypassing: wires and multiplexers that route a result from a pipeline register straight to the ALU inputs, before it reaches the register file. It removes most data-hazard stalls.
example: With forwarding, an add followed by a dependent sub needs zero stalls.

definition: Control logic that compares the source registers of the instruction entering EX with the destinations in EX/MEM and MEM/WB, and selects a forwarded value when they match (preferring the newest, and ignoring x0).

A data hazard where an instruction needs a value loaded by the instruction just before it. The data only arrives at the end of MEM, so even with forwarding one stall cycle is needed in the five-stage pipeline.
Logic in the ID stage that spots a load-use hazard and stalls: it freezes the PC and IF/ID and inserts a bubble into ID/EX.
A compiler reordering independent instructions to avoid stalls, for example by moving an unrelated instruction between a load and its use.
A register that always reads as zero and ignores writes, x0 in RISC-V and register 0 in MIPS. Forwarding logic must not forward values "written" to it.
Discarding wrongly fetched or speculatively executed instructions, turning them into bubbles, typically after a mispredicted branch or an exception.
An instruction that can change which instruction runs next. A conditional branch is taken (jumps to its target) or not taken (falls through) depending on a condition.
A branch is taken when it jumps to its target, and not taken when execution falls through to the next instruction.
The address a branch jumps to when it is taken.
Guessing a branch's direction (and target) before it is resolved, so fetch can continue without waiting. Wrong guesses are flushed, costing a misprediction penalty.
A wrong branch prediction. The processor must discard the wrong-path work and refetch from the correct path.
example: At 95% accuracy, 5 in every 100 branches mispredict.

definition: The fraction of branches a predictor gets wrong: 1 minus its accuracy. Multiplied by the branch fraction and the misprediction penalty, it gives the extra cycles per instruction lost to mispredictions.
example: A 95% accurate predictor has a misprediction rate of 5%; with 20% branches and a 15-cycle penalty that adds 0.2 × 0.05 × 15 = 0.15 to CPI.

definition: The cycles lost recovering from a mispredicted branch, roughly how many stages lie between fetch and where the branch resolves.
example: A 15-cycle penalty on 1% of instructions adds 0.15 to CPI.

definition: Prediction by a fixed rule that does not learn from history, such as always predicting not taken, or backward taken, forward not taken.
Backward taken, forward not taken: a static rule that predicts backward branches (usually loops) taken and forward branches not taken.
A small table of predictor entries, typically 2-bit counters, indexed by low bits of the branch's PC (and sometimes history). Each entry remembers how branches mapping there behaved.
A predictor entry that stores only the last outcome and predicts it again. It mispredicts twice per loop: at the exit and on re-entry.
A predictor entry holding 0 to 3: taken counts up, not taken counts down, stopping at the ends, and it predicts taken at 2 or 3. A single surprise from a strong state does not flip its prediction.
Resistance to change: a 2-bit counter in a strong state needs two opposite outcomes before its prediction flips.
Two different branches (or histories) mapping to the same predictor entry and disturbing each other's counters, because the table is indexed by only some bits.
A shift register recording the outcomes of the most recent branches, one bit each (1 = taken). Predictors combine it with the PC to learn correlated patterns.
A register whose bits move along by one position each time a new bit is shifted in, so it holds the last few bits seen.
A branch predictor (McFarling, 1993) that XORs the global history register with the branch's PC to index a table of 2-bit counters, so the same branch uses different counters in different contexts.
example: PC bits 1011 XOR history 0110 select counter 1101, entry 13.

definition: Exclusive or: a bitwise operation whose result bit is 1 when exactly one of the two input bits is 1. Written ⊕ in formulas and ^ in Python and C.
A branch predictor that runs two or more predictors (such as local and global history) and uses a trained chooser to pick which one to trust for each branch.

TAgged GEometric history length predictor (Seznec and Michaud, 2006): a base predictor plus tagged tables using geometrically increasing history lengths, so long histories are used only where they help.

A branch predictor (Jiménez and Lin, 2001) built from perceptrons: a perceptron is a simple learned model that multiplies each input by a trained weight, adds a bias and predicts from the sign of the sum. Here the inputs are recent branch outcomes; a single perceptron can only learn linearly separable patterns.
A cache indexed by PC that remembers which addresses hold branches and where they went last time, so fetch can redirect before the branch is even decoded.

A small hardware stack that predicts return targets: calls push their return address and returns pop it. Its size is limited, so a call chain deeper than the stack overwrites or loses the oldest entries, and those returns may then be mispredicted.
A predictor for jumps whose target comes from a register (virtual calls, switch jump tables, interpreter dispatch), choosing among several targets using the PC and history.
An instruction slot after a branch that executes whatever the branch does, an architectural feature of classic MIPS. The compiler fills it with useful work or a nop. RISC-V and ARM64 have none.
An instruction that selects between two values based on a condition without branching, such as x86 cmov or ARM64 csel. Useful for unpredictable conditions.
Code written to compute a result without conditional branches, for example with a conditional move or arithmetic on a comparison result. Not always faster: measure.
Compiler hints (GCC/Clang __builtin_expect, C++20 [[likely]] and [[unlikely]]) telling the compiler which way a condition usually goes, so it can lay out the likely path to fall through.
Compiling a program, running it on typical input to record which paths and branches are hot, then recompiling using that profile.
An interpreter technique where each opcode handler ends with its own indirect jump to the next handler, instead of all returning to one central switch.
A table of code addresses indexed by a value, used to compile a switch statement into one indirect jump.
A family of CPU vulnerabilities (2018) in which an attacker mistrains branch predictors so the victim speculatively executes code that leaks secrets through side effects such as cache state.
A 2018 CPU vulnerability that let some processors speculatively read kernel memory from user code and leak it through the cache before the permission check took effect.
A processor that can start more than one instruction per cycle, so CPI can fall below 1.
How many instructions a core can start (or decode, or retire) per cycle. A 4-wide core has an ideal CPI of 0.25.
How many instructions in a stretch of code could run at the same time because they do not depend on each other. Limited by true dependences, branches and memory latency.
Executing instructions as soon as their operands and a functional unit are ready, rather than strictly in program order, while still retiring them in order.
Starting instructions strictly in program order, so one stalled instruction holds up all younger ones, even independent ones.
The part of a core that fetches, decodes and (in out-of-order cores) renames instructions and feeds them to the back end. Guided by the branch predictor.
Mapping each architectural register written to a fresh physical register, so different versions of the same name can exist at once. Removes WAR and WAW dependences.
A register named by the instruction set, such as x1 to x31 in RISC-V, as opposed to the larger pool of physical registers inside the core.
One of the actual storage registers in a core that renames; there are more of them than architectural registers.
The renaming table that maps each architectural register to the physical register holding its newest value.
A list of resources that are currently unused and available to hand out. In register renaming, it holds the physical registers not holding a live value; renaming takes one for each new destination.
The state software can observe as defined by the ISA: registers, memory, the PC. Out-of-order cores update it only at in-order retirement.
An out-of-order scheduling scheme (Robert Tomasulo, IBM System/360 Model 91, 1967) using reservation stations, producer tags and a common data bus. Tags rename registers implicitly.
A 1960s IBM high-performance mainframe whose floating-point unit introduced Tomasulo's algorithm.
In Tomasulo's algorithm, a buffer in front of a functional unit holding a waiting instruction and, for each operand, either its value (V) or the tag (Q) of the station that will produce it.
In Tomasulo's algorithm, a table recording which reservation station tag will write each register next, blank if the register file value is current.
In Tomasulo's algorithm, the bus that broadcasts each result as a (tag, value) pair to every reservation station and the register file at once.

In Tomasulo's algorithm, the name of the reservation station that will produce a value. A waiting instruction holds the tag instead of the value, and grabs the value when a matching (tag, value) pair is broadcast; this renames registers implicitly.

In a CPU, a circular queue holding in-flight instructions in program order. Results wait there until each instruction reaches the head and retires, giving precise exceptions and safe recovery from mispredictions. (Network stacks use the same name for a buffer that puts out-of-order packets back in sequence.)
The final step of an instruction in an out-of-order core: committing its result to architectural state, in program order.
An exception is precise when every instruction before the faulting one has completed and none after it has changed architectural state. Imprecise exceptions break this.
Executing instructions before knowing they are needed, usually past a predicted branch. Wrong-path results are discarded, though microarchitectural traces such as cache state can remain.
A queue that holds stores, with their addresses and data, until they commit to the cache, and lets later loads forward data from matching older stores.

Supplying a load's value directly from an older store still waiting in the store buffer, when they access the same address, instead of waiting for the store to reach the cache. Real cores may require matching size and alignment.
Working out whether a load and an older store refer to the same address, letting loads speculatively pass stores with unknown addresses and replaying if they conflict.
Having several cache misses outstanding at once so their latencies overlap.
Very long instruction word: an architecture in which the compiler groups independent operations into one wide instruction, moving scheduling from hardware to software.
Explicitly parallel instruction computing, the design behind Intel Itanium: compiler-formed instruction bundles and groups, plus predication and speculation features.
Making an instruction's effect conditional on a predicate bit instead of branching around it.
The scheduler logic of an out-of-order core: compare each broadcast result tag with waiting operands (wakeup), then choose which ready instructions issue (select).
A binary format for real numbers with a fraction and an exponent, handled by dedicated floating-point units.
The point where power delivery and heat removal, rather than transistor speed, limit how fast a chip can run. It pushed designs toward multicore and efficiency from the mid-2000s.
Power used charging and discharging circuit capacitances as transistors switch, approximately activity × capacitance × voltage² × frequency.
Power that leaks through transistors even when they are not switching. It depends on voltage, temperature and transistor design.
In the dynamic power formula, the average fraction of the modelled capacitance charged per clock cycle, between 0 and 1.
How much electric charge a node stores per volt, measured in farads. Each time a transistor switches it must charge or discharge it, which costs energy.
The voltage powering a circuit, in volts. In a CMOS chip, dynamic power rises with its square, so lowering it saves a lot of power.
Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor: the transistor technology used in almost all processors. It uses power mainly when switching, plus leakage.
Metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor, the switch that CMOS chips are built from.
The gate voltage at which a transistor turns on. Lowering it lets the supply voltage fall but increases leakage.

The 1974 result (Dennard and colleagues, IBM) that shrinking a MOSFET's dimensions and its voltage together by a factor k keeps power density constant while making transistors faster. The ideal relationship broke down around the mid-2000s, when voltage could no longer keep scaling.
example: With k = 0.7, power per transistor falls to 0.49 while transistors per area rise about 2.04 times.

definition: Gordon Moore's observation that the number of transistors on a chip doubled roughly every two years.
Power per unit area of chip, for example watts per square millimetre. It decides how hard the chip is to cool.
A chip with several processor cores. It can raise throughput per watt for parallel work but does not speed up a serial task.
The speedup limit for a fixed-size job when only part of it can run in parallel: 1 / ((1 − p) + p / n). The serial part caps the speedup at 1 / (1 − p).
example: 90% parallel code on 8 cores gives about 4.7×, and never more than 10×.

definition: A more optimistic view of parallel speedup that assumes the problem size grows with the number of processors, so the parallel part dominates.
Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling: changing a processor's voltage and frequency at run time between supported operating points to trade speed for power.
Running cores above their base frequency when power, current and thermal limits allow. Intel calls it Turbo Boost.
Running a task as fast as possible and then entering a low-power idle state, which can use less total energy than running slowly when static power is significant.
Switching off the clock to idle logic so it stops switching, saving dynamic power but not leakage.
Disconnecting the supply to an idle block to cut its leakage, at the cost of time and energy to switch back on.
A processor combining fast, power-hungry cores with slower, efficient ones, so the operating system can place each task where it uses least energy for its needs.
An operating-system scheduler that uses a model of each core's energy cost to choose where to run tasks.
Chip area that cannot all run at full performance at the same time because of the power budget. Described in a 2011 study by Esmaeilzadeh and colleagues.
A specialised unit, such as a GPU or video encoder, that performs particular workloads more efficiently than a general-purpose core.
Work done per unit of energy, the key efficiency measure once power limits a design.
Turning a loop into SIMD instructions that process several data elements per instruction, which reduces instruction count.
Replicating a loop body several times per iteration to cut loop-control instructions, at the cost of bigger code.
The unit of frequency: one cycle per second.
10⁹ hertz: a billion cycles per second. A 3 GHz clock has a period of about 0.333 ns.
One billionth of a second, 10⁻⁹ s.
One trillionth of a second, 10⁻¹² s; 1,000 ps is 1 ns. This module's example pipeline stages take 100 to 300 ps.
The unit of power: one joule of energy per second.
The unit of voltage (electrical potential difference).
The unit of capacitance: one coulomb of charge per volt.
The power a base must be raised to to give a number: log₂(1,024) = 10.
The two most widely used open-source C and C++ compilers.
A family of RISC instruction sets from Arm Ltd, used in most phones and microcontrollers, in 32-bit versions and the 64-bit ARM64 (AArch64).

Bits produced by instruction decode that tell later pipeline stages what to do, such as whether to read memory or write a register. They travel with the instruction through the pipeline registers; zeroing them turns a slot into a bubble.

The set of in-flight instructions an out-of-order core can examine and schedule at once, bounded by structures such as the reorder buffer and schedulers. A bigger window can find more independent work during a long cache miss.
The maximum power a chip may draw, set by what its power delivery and cooling can handle. Under a fixed budget, more power for one part means less for another.
In a load or store such as lw x1, 8(x2), the register (x2) whose value is added to the offset (8) to form the memory address.
In a circuit, the slowest chain of logic between two registers. Its delay sets the minimum clock period, so shortening it allows a faster clock.

A performance-analysis method from Intel (Ahmad Yasin, 2014) that uses performance counters to sort a core's pipeline slots into four top-level categories: front-end bound, bad speculation, back-end bound and retiring. It shows where the lost cycles go.
